Yes, this looks much more like a database/search-indexing problem than an agent-docs problem. The docs fix helps agents avoid the slow path, but the underlying table is probably missing the right indexes for the way we search it.

> AGENT

For Hivemind specifically, the slow queries are likely because we’re doing `ilike.*term*` over `content`. A normal Postgres btree index will not help much with leading-wildcard searches like: ```sql content ILIKE '%VACE%' ``` That usually needs one of these: ```sql CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY message_feed_content_trgm_idx ON message_feed USING gin (content gin_trgm_ops); ``` Also useful: ```sql CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY message_feed_channel_created_idx ON message_feed (channel_name, created_at DESC); CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY message_feed_author_created_idx ON message_feed (author_name, created_at DESC); ``` If we want proper full-text search instead of substring search, we should add a generated/search column and GIN index: ```sql CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY message_feed_content_fts_idx ON message_feed USING gin (to_tsvector('english', content)); ``` Then query with `fts`/`plfts` only after confirming PostgREST uses that expression/index cleanly. So: not fundamentally bad to expose this via PostgREST, but broad all-channel substring search without trigram/full-text indexes will be slow. The UX fix is: add trigram + channel/date indexes, keep queries channel-scoped by default, and avoid huge `or=(content.ilike...)` searches unless the DB has the trigram index.

Is there some kind of deeper reasons these fixes like a missing abstraction or a missing tool or is it just stuff that we need to patch up to get it working? Like are we getting to the root of the issue basically?

> AGENT

Yes, there are deeper reasons. This was not just a pile of one-off bugs. The main missing abstractions are: 1. **Workflow port contract** We need a first-class way to say: this Reigh task param maps to this Comfy node input, this media input maps here, this output must be produced here, this frame count/fps/resolution must match. Right now too much of that lives in ad hoc scratchpad code and human inspection. 2. **Required connection / required input validator** The `PointsEditor` and frame-length issues should have been caught before live RunPod. VibeComfy should validate required Comfy/custom-node inputs, unbound template controls, output nodes, and artifact paths before burning GPU time. 3. **Output artifact contract** The `output/Wanimate_00001_.mp4` issue showed that VibeComfy and the worker did not share a strong artifact contract. We’ve improved this, but the real abstraction is: every workflow declares expected output type, save node, output directory, filename discovery strategy, and media validation requirements. 4. **Route parity manifest** We need one source of truth per route: WGP behavior, VibeComfy template, app params, worker params, expected outputs, live proof status, and known non-parities. The docs now approximate this, but it should be machine-readable and testable. 5. **Run/pod introspection** We had heartbeats but weak Comfy progress visibility. The inspect command helps, but the deeper missing tool is a proper “what is this live generation doing?” view: process state, Comfy stdout/stderr, active node, artifact directory growth, recent file mtimes, GPU utilization, and task DB state in one place. 6. **Workflow import/conversion tooling** A lot of drag came from adapting UI JSON/custom-node workflows into our Python-esque VibeComfy template format. That should be a toolchain: ingest workflow, preserve dict widgets, infer model assets, identify required nodes, emit a draft Python template, then validate it against Reigh route contracts. So: the individual fixes were necessary, but the pattern is clear. We are getting closer to the root by turning repeated failure modes into harness/tooling improvements. The next root-level move is to formalize **route/workflow contracts** and make port-check validation enforce them before live execution. That would prevent most of the failures we hit: missing inputs, wrong save path, wrong frame count, wrong model directory, and unclear live state.

> AGENT

I’ll quickly verify the workspace layout so I can answer this concretely rather than from memory.

> AGENT

VibeComfy is currently a separate sibling repo/package in the workspace, not a normal tracked submodule of the top-level repo. How `reigh-worker` interacts with it today: - Worker does **not import VibeComfy directly** in routing code. - For VibeComfy routes, `reigh-worker` builds scratchpad Python and runs: ```bash python3.11 -m vibecomfy.cli run <workflow_ref> --runtime embedded --ensure-packs --ensure-models ``` - It finds VibeComfy through `VIBECOMFY_CWD` / `VIBECOMFY_PATH` / `PYTHONPATH`. - Live RunPod validation clones and installs VibeComfy separately, usually from `megaplan/production-parity-templates`. What makes sense long term: - Treat VibeComfy as a **separately versioned runtime/tooling package**, not as copied code inside `reigh-worker`. - Pin it explicitly in production, ideally by git SHA or release version, so a worker image/run knows exactly which VibeComfy behavior and templates it has. - Keep the boundary stable: `reigh-worker` owns Reigh task semantics, route selection, WGP parity contracts, uploads/downloads, DB status; VibeComfy owns Comfy workflow IR, template conversion, validation, custom-node/model checks, and execution. - Avoid making it a git submodule unless we truly want top-level workspace pinning. Submodules add friction, and this workspace already has a broken gitlink-style situation for another path. A pinned package/install ref is cleaner for production. The weak point right now is that the relationship is too implicit: route support says “VibeComfy supported”, but there is not yet a strong shared contract saying “this template consumes LoRA/control/interpolation/model-selection params.” That is the abstraction I think we need next: a VibeComfy route capability manifest consumed by `reigh-worker` route selection.

From there, 100% coverage is a gated loop: 1. **Inventory everything** Extract every app-created task/capability from `reigh-app`, Supabase functions, worker registry, and live matrix. No route is allowed to be “implicit.” 2. **Classify every route** Each route gets one status: - `vibecomfy_parity_ready` - `vibecomfy_supported_needs_gap_closure` - `wgp_only_but_contract_validated` - `unsupported_fail_closed` - `unknown_untriaged` 3. **Generate required tests** For each route, auto-generate: - routing contract test - scratchpad/template validation test - output artifact contract test - one live smoke case - variant cases for LoRA/control/resolution/frame/profile settings 4. **Run coverage report** Coverage is not “green tests passed.” It is: - 100% of app routes inventoried - 100% classified - 100% have source references - 100% have expected behavior documented - 100% have either live proof or explicit fail-closed/WGP-only justification 5. **Close all `unknown` and `needs_gap_closure` rows** Implement missing VibeComfy support where product expects parity. For real non-Comfy paths like stitching/orchestrators, validate contract equivalence instead of forcing them into Comfy. 6. **Make CI enforce it** Add a check that fails when: - app adds a new capability not in the contract registry - route has no template/output contract - VibeComfy-supported route lacks a live proof reference - unsupported params are not fail-closed - docs/tracker are stale against generated data 7. **Final live sweep** Run the generated matrix on the consolidated branch. Anything that fails goes back through the same loop until the report has zero unknowns and zero unvalidated supported routes. So the practical path is: **contract registry → generated coverage report → generated tests/matrix → close gaps → CI gate → final full live sweep.**

> AGENT

Yes. It is both research and building. **Research** - Trace what the app can actually enqueue. - Trace Supabase function payloads and selector contracts. - Trace worker task registry and routing. - Trace Wan2GP behavior/defaults for each route. - Trace VibeComfy templates/scratchpads/custom nodes/models. - Compare live reports against the routes. **Building** - Add a machine-readable capability registry. - Add extractors that populate/check it from app + worker sources. - Add validators for workflow inputs/connections/models/outputs. - Add generated test cases and live matrix cases. - Add a report generator that updates the parity tracker. - Add CI checks so new app capabilities cannot bypass the registry. The process to get to real 100% confidence is: 1. **Freeze the definition of coverage** 100% means every app-created generation capability is either: - VibeComfy parity-ready with live proof, - WGP-only but contract-validated, - or explicitly unsupported/fail-closed with product approval. 2. **Build the registry and extractor** The extractor finds routes from app/Supabase/worker code. The registry becomes the reviewed source of truth. Any extracted route missing from the registry is a failure. 3. **Populate every capability row** Each row gets app source, task type, params, Wan2GP source behavior, VibeComfy source/template, output contract, validation state, and gaps. 4. **Generate tests and live cases** We stop hand-maintaining coverage. Tests and live matrix cases come from the registry. 5. **Run static validation** Catch missing params, broken Comfy graph inputs, missing save nodes, missing model/custom-node declarations, unsupported LoRA/control/profile combos. 6. **Run parity validation** Compare Wan2GP vs VibeComfy settings field-by-field. Differences must become implementation work or explicit fail-closed behavior. 7. **Run live validation** Execute all supported live cases and verify DB rows, storage artifacts, output media type, and probe results. 8. **Close every gap** No `unknown`, no “probably works,” no undocumented divergence. 9. **CI enforcement** Add a required check: if app/worker routes change and the registry/report/tests are stale, CI fails. Absolute confidence comes from making the inventory mechanically derived, the contract explicit, the matrix generated, and drift impossible to hide.

> DEVELOPER

And will that cover all the ways we vary each workflow - e.g. by adding loras, or different controlnets, and different adaptions? How is that aaccounted for?

> AGENT

It will only cover that if we model **variants** as first-class, not as notes on a route. The contract should have two layers: **1. Capability** Example: `wan_2_2_i2v`, `qwen_image_edit`, `travel_segment_wan22_vace`. This defines the base path: - task type - app entrypoints - Wan2GP handler - VibeComfy template/scratchpad - baseline model/settings - output contract **2. Variants** Each capability has a variant matrix describing every axis the app can vary: - `loras`: none, one LoRA, multiple LoRAs, URL LoRA, phase-scheduled LoRA, lightning LoRA - `control`: none, raw video, flow, canny, depth, pose, mask, annotated mask - `source media`: text-only, image-to-image, first/last images, video source, mask image - `model/profile`: Wan 2.2 T2I, Wan 2.2 I2V, VACE, LTX, Qwen 2512, Flux Klein variant - `dimensions`: default, app selectable sizes, capped sizes - `timing`: frame count, FPS, interpolation, stitch/postprocess - `prompting`: prompt, negative prompt, style prompt, empty prompt, expanded prompt - `output`: image, video, stitched video, postprocessed video Each variant gets one of these outcomes: - `supported_same_as_wgp` - `supported_with_documented_difference` - `unsupported_fail_closed` - `wgp_only` - `not_app_exposed` Then the generator creates tests from the variant matrix: - one baseline smoke per capability - one case per meaningful variant axis - pairwise/selected combinations where axes interact, like `VACE + depth + video_source`, `Qwen edit + mask`, `Wan I2V + LoRA`, `video_enhance + interpolation` We should not brute-force every possible combination because that explodes. The right engineering approach is **risk-based combinatorial coverage**: - every individual axis value covered at least once - every known interaction covered explicitly - every unsupported combination fail-closed with a test - every app-exposed option mapped to either supported behavior or an explicit block So yes, LoRAs/controlnets/adaptations are accounted for by the variant layer. Without that, the tracker would only prove “happy path per template,” not app parity.

> DEVELOPER

And will it work for adding additional workflows? Like if the community adds them? is it the right abstraction for when we and others add all kinds of new workflows?

> AGENT

Yes, if we design it as a **workflow onboarding contract**, not just a migration checklist. For any new workflow, internal or community-contributed, the contract should require: - **Identity**: capability id, task type, template id, owner/source. - **Provenance**: original workflow URL/file, author/repo, license if known, local adaptations. - **Runtime requirements**: custom nodes, model files, VAE/LoRA/controlnet files, Python deps. - **Inputs**: required/optional params, media inputs, defaults, validation rules. - **Variant axes**: LoRA support, control methods, model/profile choices, resolution/frame/FPS ranges. - **Output contract**: expected file type, save node, path prefix, DB generation row, artifact probe. - **Support state**: supported, experimental, fail-closed, WGP-only, deprecated. - **Validation gates**: static graph validation, local template validation, live run, artifact validation. - **Parity notes**: if replacing an existing path, what must match; if net-new, what behavior is promised. That makes it work for community workflows because the system doesn’t assume “we know what this template means.” It forces each workflow to declare what it needs, what it supports, and how success is proven. The key abstraction is: `workflow template` is not the product capability. A workflow is an implementation of a capability, under a contract. One capability may have multiple templates, and one template may support multiple variants. The registry should model that explicitly. For community additions, the ideal flow is: 1. Import workflow/template. 2. Auto-detect nodes, required inputs, save nodes, custom nodes, model names. 3. Generate a draft contract. 4. Human/agent fills in provenance, intended app mapping, variants, and expected outputs. 5. Static validator checks graph/connectivity/requirements. 6. Live validator runs minimal smoke. 7. Only then the workflow becomes selectable in-app. So yes: this is the right abstraction if we treat it as a reusable **capability + implementation + variant + validation** system. It would make future workflow additions much less ad hoc.

It can be a clean developer experience, but only if we avoid making people hand-author giant YAML files. The clean DX should be: ```bash reigh workflow import ./workflow.json --source-url ... reigh workflow inspect image/my_new_workflow reigh workflow validate image/my_new_workflow reigh capability add image.my_feature --template image/my_new_workflow reigh capability test image.my_feature --live reigh capability report ``` The tool should auto-draft most of the contract: - nodes used - required inputs - missing connections - save/output nodes - custom node packages - likely model filenames - media output type - template id - editable params Then the developer only fills in the intent: - what app capability this implements - source/provenance - which params are exposed - which variants are supported - whether it replaces a Wan2GP path or is net-new What is missing right now: - automatic app capability inventory - workflow import/conversion to Python scratchpad/template format - static graph validator - custom-node/model requirement detector - output artifact contract validator - variant matrix generator - latest-live-report summarizer - CI check for stale/unknown capabilities What might be unnecessary: - full exhaustive combinatorial testing; use risk-based pairwise/interaction coverage instead - forcing non-generation orchestration/stitching into Comfy; validate their contracts instead - requiring every workflow to match Wan2GP if it is net-new; parity only applies to replacements - overbuilding a UI before the CLI/contract works The main thing I’d add to the plan is **scaffolding**: make the tool generate a draft contract and a failing checklist automatically. That turns onboarding from “read docs and guess” into “run import, fix the explicit failures.”

Yes, if we add an **agent build mode** alongside import mode. For agents building from scratch, the workflow should be: ```bash reigh workflow new video/wan_custom_i2v --capability wan.custom_i2v reigh workflow add-node ... reigh workflow connect ... reigh workflow set-input prompt "{{ prompt }}" reigh workflow set-output video --prefix "wan-custom" reigh workflow validate video/wan_custom_i2v reigh capability test wan.custom_i2v --live ``` But more realistically, agents should not hand-build graphs node-by-node unless necessary. The better agent DX is: 1. **Declare intent** “Build an image-to-video workflow using WanVideoWrapper with optional LoRA and first-frame input.” 2. **Tool drafts a contract** Capability id, required inputs, variant axes, expected output, model/custom-node requirements. 3. **Agent chooses a starting point** Existing ready template, community workflow, or blank template. 4. **Agent edits in Python format** The agent mutates a typed workflow object, not raw JSON. 5. **Validator catches mistakes** Missing required connections, invalid node class, unresolved model, no save node, unsupported param, wrong output path. 6. **Tool generates smoke cases** Baseline plus declared variants. 7. **Live test proves it** The capability only becomes supported after artifact validation passes. For this to work well, we need a few agent-specific affordances: - template search/discovery - “explain this workflow” output - graph diff before/after edits - required connection checker - parameter binding checker - output contract checker - source/provenance notes - generated TODOs for unsupported variants - example scratchpads by category The key is that agents need **tight feedback loops**. They should not discover missing edges or output paths only after launching a GPU run. The local/static validator must catch as much as possible before live testing. So yes: the same abstraction works for scratch-built workflows, as long as the tool supports draft, inspect, validate, diff, and live-test loops.

Whats' the right bastraction here? Why is this so messy right now if we have the functionality? What woudl a clean beautifully engineered from a high-level persepctive version look like?

> AGENT

The right abstraction is: **Capability Contract** A product capability is the stable thing. A workflow/template is just one implementation of it. Right now it is messy because the system has good pieces, but they live at the wrong levels and are not joined by a single contract. We currently have: - VibeComfy tools for template mechanics: import, port, validate, custom nodes, models, RunPod runs. - Worker tools for routing: task type, route key, backend choice, fail-closed rules. - Live-test tools for proving one case ran. - App/Supabase code that actually defines what users can ask for. - Wan2GP code that defines current behavior and defaults. The gap is that no object says: **“this app capability means these inputs, these variants, this Wan2GP behavior, this VibeComfy implementation, this output contract, and this validation evidence.”** So each layer is locally sensible, but globally implicit. That is why we keep rediscovering: - which branch/ref has the template - whether a workflow is JSON or Python scratchpad - whether LoRAs/control/video-source are supported - whether output paths are correct - whether “live green” means parity or just one happy path - whether an orchestrator/stitch path should be Comfy at all A clean version would look like this: ```text App Capability -> Capability Contract -> route semantics -> parameter schema -> variant matrix -> implementation bindings -> Wan2GP implementation -> VibeComfy template/scratchpad -> requirements -> models -> custom nodes -> input media -> output artifact contract -> validation state -> static validation -> parity review -> live proof ``` Then the tooling becomes simple: ```bash reigh capability discover reigh capability status reigh capability validate qwen.image_edit reigh capability test qwen.image_edit --live reigh capability report ``` And VibeComfy remains focused: ```bash vibecomfy port check ... vibecomfy port convert ... vibecomfy validate ... vibecomfy nodes install-plan ... vibecomfy run ... ``` **Ownership Boundary** - **VibeComfy owns**: Comfy workflow representation, JSON-to-Python conversion, graph validation, node/model requirements, ready templates, local/runtime execution. - **reigh-worker owns**: product capability contracts, routing, backend selection, Wan2GP comparison, app parameter semantics, fail-closed behavior, DB/artifact contracts, live app validation. - **reigh-app owns**: user-facing capability surface and which parameters users can actually set. **What Beautiful Looks Like** A new workflow lands like this: 1. `vibecomfy port check workflow.json` 2. `vibecomfy port convert workflow.json --ready-id image/foo` 3. `vibecomfy validate image/foo` 4. `reigh capability scaffold image.foo --template image/foo` 5. Contract generator asks for/infers: - app task type - exposed params - […]

> DEVELOPER

And do we have the centralise other capabilities? Or clean up the naming or positioning somehow? Anything we can use from the earlier VibeComfy?

> AGENT

Yes: we should centralize the **product capabilities**, but not centralize every low-level VibeComfy feature into the worker. Right now naming is messy because we have overlapping concepts: - `task_type`: DB/worker execution type, e.g. `qwen_image_edit` - `route_key`: backend-selection identity, e.g. `travel_segment__model-wan22_vace__guidance-vace_depth...` - `template_id`: VibeComfy implementation, e.g. `video/wanvideo_wrapper_22_14b_vace_cocktail` - `workflow id`: VibeComfy corpus/import identity - `case name`: live-test matrix label - `capability`: the actual product thing users care about The missing central name is **capability id**. Example shape: ```text capability: image.qwen.edit task_type: qwen_image_edit route_key: qwen_image_edit implementations: wgp: source.models.model_handlers.qwen_handler.handle_qwen_image_edit vibecomfy: edit/qwen_image_edit variants: mask: supported lora: gap style_reference: separate capability or variant ``` For travel: ```text capability: video.travel.segment.wan22_vace task_type: travel_segment [REDACTED] implementations: wgp: Wan2GP travel segment path vibecomfy: video/wanvideo_wrapper_22_14b_vace_cocktail variants: control_mode: raw | flow | canny | depth continuity: first_last | video_source lora: gap ``` **Clean Positioning** I’d use this hierarchy: ```text Capability: product behavior Route: execution decision for a capability variant Implementation: WGP or VibeComfy binding Template: VibeComfy implementation detail Workflow: source/import artifact Live case: validation sample ``` That gives us sane language: - “This capability is app-ready.” - “This route is VibeComfy-supported.” - “This template is runtime-green.” - “This variant is fail-closed.” - “This live case validates the depth/video-source route.” **What To Reuse From Earlier VibeComfy** The valuable older idea is not old code so much as its discipline: - `ready_template` must not mean `runtime_green`. - Workflow corpus status should stay explicit: raw, converted, ready template, runtime ready, runtime green. - Model staging should be registry-driven and fail loudly. - Custom-node planning belongs in VibeComfy, not worker. - Runtime assumptions should be evidence/artifacts, not stale prose. So yes, we should reuse the **status vocabulary** from VibeComfy’s corpus model, but apply it at the capability level in worker: ```text unknown inventoried routed template_bound static_valid runtime_green parity_reviewed app_ready ``` The concrete next cleanup I’d do is add a central `capability_contracts` registry in `reigh-worker`, keyed by clean capability ids, while keeping VibeComfy’s own template/workflow registries untouched. That becomes the bridge between app, worker, Wan2GP, VibeComfy, live tests, and docs.

If a developer had to rebuild this whole system from the current picture, the biggest help would be a **guided capability workbench** that tells them exactly where they are and what remains. The flow I’d want: ```bash reigh capability discover reigh capability status reigh capability inspect video.travel.segment.wan22_vace reigh capability next ``` For each capability, it should show: ```text Capability: video.travel.segment.wan22_vace App entrypoints: ... Task type: travel_segment Route variants: raw, flow, canny, depth, video_source, first_last Wan2GP source: ... VibeComfy template: video/wanvideo_wrapper_22_14b_vace_cocktail VibeComfy status: static_valid, runtime_green Parity status: needs_lora_review Live proof: scripts/live_test/runs/... Missing: dynamic LoRA variant, parent orchestration parity Next command: reigh capability validate video.travel.segment.wan22_vace --variant with_lora ``` What would be helpful: - one central capability id/name per product behavior - automatic source references into app, worker, Wan2GP, VibeComfy - generated variant matrix - generated live-test cases - clear status labels - “next best action” commands - workflow/template diff in product terms - output artifact validation baked in - fail-closed reasons shown as first-class state What would still be awkward: - Wan2GP behavior is not naturally declarative, so extracting exact defaults/settings may require code tracing. - App capability discovery across frontend + Supabase functions can be noisy unless we define clear enqueue boundaries. - Some routes are orchestration/stitching, not Comfy workflows, so “parity” means DB/artifact contract parity rather than template parity. - LoRA/control variants can explode combinatorially unless we use explicit risk-based variant coverage. - Live GPU validation will remain slow/expensive, so the local static validators need to catch almost everything before launch. The clean rebuild would not start with templates. It would start with: ```text What can the app ask for? What route does that become? What behavior does Wan2GP provide today? What implementation provides that in VibeComfy? What variants are allowed? How do we prove it? ``` Then templates become replaceable implementation details instead of the thing everyone reasons from.

That avoids creating another manual thing developers must update every time. The tool should derive as much as possible from the workflow itself, then only require explicit metadata where inference is unsafe.

The same gates apply, but the entry point differs. A clean model would be: ```text Start from anything -> identify intent -> choose source/fork/create path -> run structural/schema checks -> declare requirements -> expose semantic patch points -> validate locally -> validate in app/worker contract if needed -> run on RunPod -> record evidence ``` For an **existing workflow**, the checklist is more like: - Load it with `load_workflow_any`. - Inspect current metadata, requirements, patch points, output contract. - Run `doctor --strict-ready-template`. - Compare against current live Comfy schema. - If changing behavior, update tests and parity contract. - Run focused local tests. - Run focused RunPod case. - Record evidence. For a **fork**, we need one extra decision gate: - Is this a **recipe/patch** or a **new ready template**? Rule of thumb: - If it decorates the same handles and is just a task-specific run configuration, use a recipe or patch. - If it changes graph shape, model family, required inputs, output semantics, custom nodes, or app capability, create a new ready template. That should be documented directly because otherwise people will fork templates unnecessarily or hide major behavior changes in runtime patch code. For **from scratch**, same process, but no `port check` source JSON. Instead: - author with `VibeWorkflow`/blocks - run `validate` - run `doctor` - require model/node/output metadata before promotion - add manifest/index if it becomes a ready template So I’d position the doc as: **“Workflow Lifecycle: create, fork, fix, or promote a workflow.”** Not “Adding Templates And Models.” The CLI could mirror that: ```bash vibecomfy workflow check <id-or-path> vibecomfy workflow fork video/foo --new-id video/foo_lora vibecomfy workflow promote out/scratchpads/foo.py --ready-id video/foo vibecomfy workflow readiness video/foo --strict ``` But implementation can stay lightweight at first: update the skill/AGENTS docs and make existing commands the checklist. Then add a wrapper command once the process is stable.

SageAttention is definitely a valid option on 4090-class machines, but it is not a trivial `pip install` switch for this exact RunPod image. The public package notes it is optimized for 4090/3090, while the newer wheels are tightly coupled to CUDA/PyTorch/GPU architecture; several current install paths require matching PyTorch/CUDA wheels or building CUDA kernels for the specific architecture.

> AGENT

We can install `sageattention`, but I wouldn’t make every workflow depend on it by default. The right fundamental approach is two profiles: - **Portable/default RunPod profile:** use `sdpa` + `fp16`, no SageAttention requirement. This should always validate on our standard worker image and is the safe parity baseline. - **Optimized 4090 profile:** install and validate `sageattention` explicitly, then allow `sageattn` / Sage patch nodes only when that profile is active. Why not only install it? - `sageattention` is hardware/CUDA/PyTorch sensitive. The package is optimized for 4090/3090, but newer versions/wheels need matching CUDA, PyTorch, Python, and GPU architecture combinations. - Our current RunPod image is `pytorch:2.4.0 + CUDA 12.4`. Some SageAttention paths expect newer PyTorch/CUDA or compile kernels during install. - We just saw a live failure where the template assumed SageAttention existed but the environment contract did not. That means the workflow was under-declared. So the fix should be: 1. Keep portable templates from silently requiring SageAttention. 2. Add a declared `runtime_profile: sageattention_4090` or similar. 3. Make the installer/preflight install and verify it for that profile: `python -c "import sageattention"` plus a tiny Comfy schema/runtime check. 4. Only allow `attention_mode='sageattn'` when the profile passed. That gives us performance where available without making baseline validation fragile. Sources: PyPI notes SageAttention is optimized for RTX 4090/3090, and the upstream/project ecosystem documents CUDA/PyTorch/architecture-specific install constraints. https://pypi.org/project/sageattention/ https://github.com/thu-ml/SageAttention

> AGENT

Yes. This exposed a real deeper issue: we had conflated three identities that need to stay separate. `task_type` is the app capability, like `wan_2_2_i2v`. `model` is the backend-loadable model identity, which for WGP must be something Wan2GP can load, like `wan_2_2_i2v_lightning_baseline_2_2_2`. `template_id` is the VibeComfy implementation choice, like `video/wanvideo_wrapper_22_14b_i2v_kijai`. Those are not smoothly interchangeable if they share one field. The well-engineered version is exactly what we’re moving toward: app code asks for a capability, routing selects a backend, then each backend receives its own native execution identity. WGP should never see a Comfy template id as `model`; VibeComfy should never require a Wan2GP default json as its template. The contract should verify those boundaries before live runs. I’ve fixed the immediate catalog leak and added a regression test, but I’m still validating the live retry now to prove the fix on RunPod.

> AGENT

I found the likely root cause: the earlier shutdown timeout wrapped `Comfy.__aexit__` in `asyncio.wait_for`, which runs the coroutine in a different asyncio context. Comfy’s own context manager later resets a `ContextVar` token created during `__aenter__`, so the reset fails and suppresses the successful run result before metadata is printed. The proper fix is to keep `__aexit__` in the original context and put the timeout around the slow cleanup future inside Comfy’s embedded client instead.

> AGENT

> DEVELOPER

So what would the 'proper' solution ehre look liek taht would sovle this + other problems?

> AGENT

The proper solution is a workflow runtime contract that is generated from the Python workflow, not maintained as a separate spreadsheet. It should have one canonical object with these sections: `assets` (models/input fixtures/output paths), `nodes` (required packs and pinned versions), `python_packages` (SageAttention-ada, onnxruntime, etc.), `runtime_flags` (`--use-sage-attention`, memory profile, cache policy), `schema_requirements` (required inputs and accepted node widgets), and `evidence` (last RunPod GPU, wall time, generation time, VRAM peak, output artifacts, media checks). Then every tool uses that same object: - `vibecomfy doctor` validates required inputs, node schemas, packages, model paths, output saves, and pure-Python policy before runtime. - `vibecomfy reconcile` installs/stages declared models, node packs, and Python packages into the target environment. - `reigh live-test` refuses to queue work until the contract is satisfied, and records timing/VRAM/output evidence back into the contract evidence log. - Astrid consumes the output-artifact contract, fetches generated media, and runs image/video-understanding checks against route-specific expectations. That would have prevented this specific issue because the LTX template enabling `PathchSageAttentionKJ(auto)` would have declared `sageattention` and the preflight would either install SageAttention-ada or fail before the app task ran. It also covers missing models, wrong model folders, missing required node inputs, JSON-vs-Python violations, missing output files, and “it ran but produced the wrong kind of artifact.”

> AGENT

We do have conversion tools. The problem is they mostly convert JSON into **literal Python graph construction**, not into a clean semantic workflow API. Current tools: - `tools/convert_ready_templates.py` Converts legacy `API_WORKFLOW` / `NODES` templates into Python files. - `vibecomfy.porting.emitter.emit_ready_template_python` Emits `wf.node(...)` calls with preserved node IDs and edges. - `tools/format_as_python.py` Older/compat emitter path for formatting a workflow as Python. - `vibecomfy.porting.workbench` Inspects/imports workflow JSON, analyzes assets, custom nodes, widgets, and porting issues. - `ready_template_source_info(...)` Detects whether a template is pure Python, JSON reference, JSON runtime wrapper, etc. - `test_ready_templates_are_pure_python_builders` Catches obvious “JSON blob embedded in Python” regressions. Why they’re incomplete: They answer “can this JSON be materialized as Python?” but not “is this now a pleasant, semantic, editable workflow?” The generated output is still basically: ```python _node(wf, "LTXVImgToVideoConditionOnly", "4970", ...) wf.replace_edge("4970.image", ...) ``` That is technically pure Python, but it is still node-ID-level graph surgery. It does not give us first-class concepts like: ```python workflow.stage(1).condition_on(start_image, strength=1.0) workflow.stage(2).condition_on(end_image, strength=1.0) workflow.set_wan2gp_sigmas(...) workflow.expose_reigh_patch_points(...) ``` So the missing layer is a **semantic workflow authoring/editing layer** on top of the converted graph. Why I ended up doing “JSON hacking shit”: The compiled Comfy payload is JSON-shaped because Comfy executes JSON-shaped node graphs. I used compiled API assertions in a test to verify links. That was the wrong level for the test. It made the test read like compiled JSON is the source of truth, when the source of truth should be the Python `VibeWorkflow`. Correct approach from here: - Use converted templates only as raw material. - Build/maintain app-facing workflows as pure Python templates. - Add helpers/contracts that assert graph semantics from `VibeWorkflow`, not raw compiled API blobs. - Compile to API only as a final runtime smoke check. - Add a validator that fails if a ready template embeds `API_WORKFLOW`, calls `workflow_from_api`, loads JSON at runtime, or relies on JSON wrappers. So: the tools exist, but they stop one level too low. We need to add the missing semantic workflow editing/validation layer, and I should use that instead of testing or patching through raw compiled API links.
